We have a picture that will be assessed sometime later. I'm just asking what you saw to compare it with your statement. Now we've come to this part that I wanted to show you. For the first time in your statement you mentioned in this paragraph below the mosque that you had seen Stanko and Buda Milkovic wearing police uniforms. That's the first time you stated that in your 1999 statement. Tell me, before that time did they wear such uniforms as well, or was it only then that they started wearing police uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: I didn't see them earlier in uniforms. It was during this time that I saw them in uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's apology, didn't turn on the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Nothing has been heard of what you said then. Could you repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I said, you knew Stavro Velickovic, who you mentioned here in the statement, you knew him at that time, didn't you? That's something you mentioned in the statement, Stavro Velickovic and other persons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: I knew them as people from Zheger village. I lived in Vlladove, myself, but attended school in Zheger. So we knew the people who lived in the surrounding villages. So these people that I've mentioned here by names are people from Zheger village who accompanied the police and the army and were with them when they committed the massacres in the villages I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, this was a question that you could have easily answered with a yes, and then I can explain why I asked this question, because this Stavro Velickovic is mentioned in another statement. I want to ask you: Did you discuss this with Qamil Shabani?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: No, never. He describes the events that -- the way he experienced them in his statement. I described the events the way I experienced them in my statement. There is no link between the two statements. He has his own; I have mine. If you're saying so, then probably he saw him as well, the way I saw him, that is, Stavro Velickovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, but when he was giving a statement in 2001, he didn't know Stavro Velickovic, and he found out his name in 2006. And since the two of you talked and you know his name, I thought that perhaps you told him. That's why I asked if you had talked. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: I gave a statement in 1999 and I provided all these names at that time. I don't know what he said in his statement. I have my statement. I'm here at your disposal for any questions that you have about my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the same page two paragraphs below you say: "After two weeks spent in the hills we ran short of food, and I went to Presevo ..." Tell me, did you go alone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: I went alone to Presheve with a friend of mine. He took a tractor to collect my family and take it to Presheve; however, when we got there we realised that the army had surrounded the hill where the entire population was staying and that they had directed part of the population on tractors to Presheve. There I saw three persons carrying their father in a blanket, father who was ill. The army fired and killed the old man --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... we'll come to that. Thank you. We'll come to that. That comes next. But let me ask you, did you go to get your own tractor in Presevo, or did you go for your friend, to get his tractor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: I went to a friend of mine to see and learn from him what the situation was in Presheve and to ask for his tractor to collect my family, but this didn't happen because the police and the army had surrounded the hill where the population was staying.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You mean it didn't happen in Presevo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: I'm talking about Kodra e Zeze and the villages in that mountainous area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't quite understand, but let's move on. Tell me, was your sister at Presevo then when you went?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: My sister lives in Presheve with her family. She is married there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the next paragraph you say: "The following morning my friend and I got onto his tractor and went to the village where my family was staying ..." Is that correct? Did you hear my question, or didn't you understand it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... paragraph I'm reading the sentence to you: "The next morning my friend and I took his tractor and went to the village where my family was staying ..." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And in this paragraph we read your family was in the village.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: In Llastice, which is in the mountain.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. Let me find the English version to get this right. Here I found it: [In English] "The next morning I and my friend took his tractor and went to the village where my family was staying." [Interpretation] That's the statement you signed that was interpreted back to you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: I think I'm very clear, but I think you refuse to understand me correctly. I'm always talking about Llastice village which is part of the hill or mountain Kodra e Zeze where we stayed. So I always refer to Llastice village. I went to collect my family in Llastice village, but what happened in the meantime was that the police and army had surrounded Kodra e Zeze, they had collected all the population that was there, and directed part of them towards Presheve. My family was in that part. The following day I met my family in Presheve.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness, but I think the person who took this statement - and I too - make a distinction between the mountain and the village. If Vlastica is a village on the mountain and therefore you say that they are in the mountains, that's different, but I understood you differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it's time for the break, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will have our second break now, Mr. Djurdjic, and resume at 1.00. You have had an extremely long time with this witness. We would ask that you finish this witness in the course of the next session, allowing a quarter of an hour for re-examination. Thank you. We adjourn now for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, we came to the point where you got back from Presevo and you saw a large number of tractors carrying people from neighbouring villages going towards Presevo; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you were going from Presevo towards Vlastica; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: This was a day before I left Presheve. The Serb police and army pushed us out. One -- one part of the population went towards Presheve, and from there towards Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I haven't come to that yet. When you were first going back from Presevo you saw convoys - that's paragraph 21 in your statement number -- it's page 9 in Albanian and page -- page 8 in English. You set out from Presevo and saw these columns of people and vehicles. Is that correct, what it says in this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You say my friend and I were hiding and observing. Why were you hiding?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: Of course we were hiding. How could we face the army to be shot at? What do you think? Whoever they came across they beat them, they massacred them, they maltreated them. So we were hiding and we were following what was going on, and some of the families, of our families, had gone on tractors and -- towards Presheve.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm interested now in this part of your statement where you say that you knew one of the three men, his name was Fazli Rrustemi, and then in your 16 November 2006 statement you said his name was Fazli Ukshini. Is it true his name was Fazli Ukshini?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: Yes, Fazli Ukshini. But there is a mistake in the statement. And it says -- the statement says Fazli Rrustemi. That is why I have made an improvement, a correction on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Please, don't waste our time. That's what I said. You corrected it, and you said his name was in fact Fazli Ukshini. Is this person related to the Ukshini that we had mentioned earlier today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: No. That person who we earlier mentioned as one who was killed, his first name was Ukshin, and they are not related.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Is the name of the person who perished Ukshin Ukshini?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: Yes, but he was from Zheger. The other one from -- the other one was from another village, and they were not related in any way. He was from Masall [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So let's get this right. We mean the Ukshini from Zegra village. Are you claiming that this Ukshin Ukshini from Zegra was killed together with his wife on the 28th of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: Yes, Ukshin Ukshini and his wife, they were killed. They lived in Zheger. They were in Naser village before, but they came to live in Zheger. And the Serbian army went to Zheger and killed them in their own home, both he and his wife were around 70 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is this Ukshini's son Musli Ukshini?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: Yes, if I'm not mistaken, he had a son by the name of Musli, Musli Ukshini.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one more thing. This Ukshin Ukshini, was he wounded before he was killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: No. I explained it very clearly in my previous statement. He was shot at by the Serb army. He had gone to the police to report it, and the police were playing with him, they didn't take it seriously, and he was killed. Then later they went on to his home and killed his wife too.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do you know if this -- do you know where this Ukshin Ukshini was buried?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: I think in the Masall village. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you say that you went to Zub village and that you spent one night with the head of one household, did that man stay in the village after you left?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: I don't know, but everyone left because the Serb army arrived, so everyone left to escape the violence of the Serb army. No one stayed behind. All the ethnic Albanian villages were emptied out. The Serbian army didn't even let us stay in the mountains nearby.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And how did you then continue from this Zub village to Presevo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: On foot, across the mountains. We travelled for about 12 hours. We had women and children with us, so we had to stop on the way, and we were fearing all the time the Serb army, and we were trying to avoid in every possible way the Serb army, who could kill us if they came across us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did you take the road, or did you go along mountain tracks with the women and children?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: Through mountains.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And while you were travelling in the column through the mountains, the police and the army didn't touch you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: They were -- they were not there at the time, because we got up to the mountains trying to avoid their presence, and once we left the villages we tried to hide from them in the mountains. There was no contact with them in the mountains.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Please, let us not waste time. Listen to my questions. When you left Zub and arrived in Presevo, according to your statement am I right to assume that you never come across either the police or the army on your way because you travelled through the mountains?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: Let me explain once again, and I will say it once again. We left Zub. We were fired on as we were leaving, the Serb army, that is, they fired on us. We left there, and we -- we joined other people who were in the mountains, and we went to the village of Sefer, and then we carried on through the mountains, cliff, hill-sides, and there was no contact with the police or the army there until we reached Presheve.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You could have just answered me with a yes. All I wanted to hear is what you told at the very end. Thank you. Tell me now, please, who from your family did you find in Presevo? Don't give me their names, just tell me how they were related to you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: As I've said earlier, it was my sister. And when we reached there I was told that my family was there. And there I learned that one of my sisters had stayed behind in the mountains. She hadn't managed to join the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I asked you about your family. You said your wife, the children. Am I right in assuming that your mother was there as well? How many sisters have reached Presevo apart from the one who had already been living there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: My two sisters, my brother, my wife with the children, my mother.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, they came from the mountain to Presevo, all these people that you have enumerated now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: Members of my family were taken by the army in tractors. They were directed by the army to go to Presheve. Myself and a group of people went on foot through mountains. We arrived in Presheve, and that's where I joined my family. At Kodra e Zeze where the population was staying, the army boarded the people on tractors. Part of the people went to Presheve and another part towards Sllatine. But there are people who have given statements pertaining to this other incident. In my statement I've described only the things that I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I see that what you are saying is being translated excellently, but tell me which members of your family were sent by the army to Presevo, and who did you find in Presevo when you arrived there who had previously been in the mountains and were at the moment of your arrival in Presevo?

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry to interrupt, but I think the witness has already answered the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I have understood him to give a detailed answer to that, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I wanted him to tell me exactly because he gave me extensive answers. He was telling me who was already in Presevo. I asked him only which members of his family arrived in Presevo in order for me to be able to ask the next question. But he persistently avoids to give me answers to specific questions that I'm interested in. And I think it is very simple. I have even given him sort of guidance. The only thing I didn't know was how many of his sisters arrived in Presevo, and I didn't know about his brother. I just asked him about how many of his sisters arrived in Presevo. That is all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Once again, sir, will you please tell us - and this will be the last time, Mr. Djurdjic - you had one sister living in Presevo. How many other sisters came to Presevo from the mountains?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two sisters, my mother, my brother, my wife and children, and others who were there. One of my sisters was married in Livor village in Kosova, whereas the third sister that did not manage to join us had remained in Kosova. The members of my family that I mentioned came from the mountains to Preshevo, and I think I was clear in my previous answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, tell me, who left Presevo along with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: I will repeat this again, although I explained it earlier. My wife, my children, my mother, my brother and sisters, and all others that had come from Kosova from those villages. We all joined the convoy and proceeded towards Macedonia escorted by the army and the police. There we were searched. Our documents were seized. We were left in the border area to wait until the Macedonian border was opened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You were only asked about the first part of that, how many of your family left with you. Now, you've got the answer, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that the family of your sister who was living in Presevo and the Albanians from Presevo didn't join you on your trip to Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: You're right, they remained in Presheve.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Witness, tell me, which of your documents was seized from you at the border?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: ID cards and passports, also driving licences.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you went to Macedonia. Where did you give your first statement upon your arrival in Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: In the refugee camp in Macedonia, in Stankovec, that's where I gave my first statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you gave that statement, did you know anything about the fate of your sister who stayed behind in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: I didn't know anything about her whereabouts for three weeks. I only knew that she remained behind in Kosova. I didn't know whether she was alive or dead. Three weeks later a group of people came to Macedonia, and that's when we all got together as a family.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know about her fate and her whereabouts on the 30th of May, 1999, when you gave your statement to an investigator?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: When I gave the statement to the investigators, she had already arrived in Macedonia with the other group. We were already together. She gave a statement of her own regarding the things that she experienced. And I gave my own statement to the investigators.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Were you present while she was giving her statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: No. She was alone when she gave her statement, and I was alone when I gave my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So between the moment when you were rejoined with her until the time when you gave statements, did you discuss anything with her about what had happened in the intervening period before she arrived in Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: Of course I discussed this with my sister, but my statement has nothing to do with her statement. I don't know what she stated in her statement. I know what is in my statement. Of course I asked her, What did you go through? And then she explained to me, described everything that happened to them from the moment they were separated from the people, how they were taken back to the village and then towards Sllatine, how they were maltreated. She remained in Sllatine for three weeks, and afterwards she came to Macedonia and joined us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And am I right to say that from Stankovec you went to Switzerland?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I put it to you that you only could have gone to Switzerland with your passport. You couldn't have gone abroad without a passport.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: No, what you're saying is not correct. The truth is that my trip there was organised by a foreign organisation. We were taken to Switzerland as refugees. We didn't have passports. We didn't have anything. We reported at Stankovec that we have a parent living in Switzerland, and that's why they took us to Switzerland. We joined the parent there without -- we didn't have any documents or anything. We stayed there for ten months or so, and then we came back to Kosova. We returned from Switzerland upon our own free will. This is the whole story. When we returned we saw evidence of the horror that had occurred in the village and the surrounding villages. I really cannot explain in words the crimes that they had committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You say that your passport was taken away from you. Can you tell me when were you issued a travel document that allows you to go abroad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: I was issued another travel document after I returned from Switzerland. We registered ourselves as residents by the local authority, as it was earlier, and then we applied for the documents. I have now the passport of Republic of Kosova, as do other free civilians in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: When was this passport of the Republic of Kosovo issued to you, the one that you have just mentioned, in what year?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: I think I have it on me. I will show it to you. This is the new passport of Republic of Kosova. It was issued to me on the 30th of January, 2009, and it's valid for ten years.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I knew that, but I wanted to know how you travelled before January 2009 and when was the first time after you returned to Kosovo that you travelled abroad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: When I returned I reported myself to the IOM, and I was issued an UNMIK passport which was valid for two years, and I used it to travel, and now I have this new passport.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right to say that whatever you saw from the mountain was the same thing that your sister saw as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: I don't know what my sister saw. I saw the things I described in my statement. In her statement you can see what she saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Witness. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have concluded my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djurdjic. Ms. D'Ascoli.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I only have a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, at page 36 of today's transcript, my learned colleague asked you about the part of your statement when you speak of those two cases you heard of, of people being killed in the village of Zegra. For the record, these cases are mentioned in the last two paragraphs of page 6 of the English version of the witness statement, and I think it's the end of page 2 and the beginning of page 3 in the B/C/S version. Sir, I just wanted to clarify, when did you hear about those cases, at which moment in time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: I heard about these cases while I was still in the village; however, when these incidents occurred in Zheger village, that the army and the police and the local Serbs entered the village and massacred people who they found in their own homes, the population started fleeing.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And by saying "I was still in the village," which village do you mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: I'm referring to Vlladove village.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. At page 52, lines 14 to 22, of today's transcript you were asked to describe what you saw with regards to the mosque, and you replied by saying that the elderly people were collected and brought to the mosque and that six persons were killed. You later clarified in your answers that you were referring to what you saw happening -- what was happening in the village of Vladovo. Sir, in relation to what you said in that -- in that answer, you said "they carried out looting, burning, and they ordered these people to bury the bodies ..." Can you just clarify to whom you were referring to when you said "they."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: "They" refers to the Serb army. The elderly people who happened to be in the village were gathered by them in front of the mosque and were kept there the whole day until their action was completed. The six persons were not killed at the mosque, but three were killed in the village and three at the entry to the village. Then these people who happened to be in the village were ordered to bury the body, and consequently they were ordered to leave. And from that day on nobody from the village dared to return.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thanks. That's enough. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You'll be pleased to know that completes the questions. The Chamber has your statements and your previous evidence and what you've been able to tell us today in answer to the questions. We would like to thank you for coming again to The Hague and assisting us with this work. You may, of course, now return to your normal activities. The court officer will show you out. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, for giving me the opportunity to come here and tell the truth. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: This could be an opportune time to mention two procedural matters, the first is Exhibit P419 which was admitted in Albanian with an English translation. We're told that a B/C/S translation has now been obtained and leave is granted to upload the B/C/S translation into Exhibit P419 so that it will become part of that exhibit. There was a second matter. The Prosecution notification of order of witnesses filed on the 9th of March will now be given the status of a confidential filing. That's because of the need to be careful about identities in the filing. A further matter. The Chamber has received today, Mr. Djurdjic, a letter from the Presiding Judge of the Belgrade District Court War Crimes Chamber, in which the Judge indicates that your client, Mr. Djordjevic, has been asked to give evidence in a trial being conducted in the War Crimes Chamber and that your client wishes to give evidence in that trial but that his problem is that he is unable to do so because of the continuous daily sittings that we have. If it is the case that your client is prepared to give evidence to the War Crimes Chamber, this Chamber would be prepared not to sit to allow that to be done. It is suggested that it would be convenient to the War Crimes Chamber if this could be arranged in the week commencing the 22nd of June and that the evidence of your client would be given here in The Hague, either by videolink or by a Judge travelling from Belgrade to hear the evidence here. Are you in a position to indicate whether it is the wish of your client that he be able to give evidence to the War Crimes Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As always, you are absolutely right, and you have given the exact and correct facts. He is willing to give evidence, and we would like to have one day for him to do so; however, we would prefer a Judge coming over here and hearing his evidence. And we already sent notice to the War Crimes Chamber that we are ready at the earliest convenient date that you grant for that purposes, we shall be ready to meet their requirements. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's very reassuring for me to hear from you that I am always right, Mr. Djurdjic. I seem to have joined the company of your assistant.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, a Court is always right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm merely giving you the content of the letter that I have received from Belgrade, so the praise should be theirs. As you confirm what Judge Krstajic has indicated, this Chamber, I think to be sure that there is no difficulty, would not sit on Thursday, the 25th of June; and Friday, the 26th, to be sure that whatever is needed with respect to the trial in Belgrade can be dealt with. Now, it's not for us whether a Judge comes from Belgrade or there is a videolink, that is a matter for the court in Belgrade. So we'll have to leave it to you and your client to arrange that. But we can indicate now that for this reason we will not sit on Thursday, the 25th of June; and Friday, the 26th of June, so that people can plan ahead for that situation. We understood, Ms. Gopalan, that there may have been a procedural matter you wished to raise.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours. It's a short matter, and I hope to finish the application in a few minutes, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I'd like to make an oral application to add an exhibit to our exhibit list, Your Honour. This exhibit is 65 ter 05258, and it's a selection of seven photographs that were taken from a book entitled: "A Village Destroyed" by Fred Abrahams. Now, this book was referred to during the testimony of Mr. Abrahams, and it is an expanded and colour version of the Human Rights Watch report of the same title which is already in evidence, and that was tendered through Mr. Abrahams. So the book and the report have the same title, but the book contains better photographs than the report. They are colour photographs. The book also contains some additional photographs that were taken as part of the same investigative process undertaken by Mr. Abrahams. I was alerted, or we were alerted to these additional photographs when the next witness, Mr. Berisha, brought the book in -- for proofing session. We are now seeking to make use of these photographs with the next two witnesses, Mr. Berisha and Mr. Kelmendi. They have been disclosed to the Defence, and we have notified them of our intention to use these photographs, so the Defence have had notice. And it's also my submission that the Chamber and all parties will benefit from clear and colour photographs that will explain or that are related to the testimony of the next two witnesses. Indeed, some of these photographs are referred to in the witness's statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can you just make one thing more clear for us. Is it that they are merely better quality and colour prints of photographs that were to be used, or are they additional and different photographs?

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honours, it's both of those. There are some photographs that are in colour and of better quality that have -- that are part of the report that have been admitted. So those are already in evidence except they are of a lower quality. There are remaining photographs, three to be precise, that are additional that we are seeking to add. So as a whole the exhibit comprises of photographs that are already in evidence and photographs that are not in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you have already resolved half of the issue in advance. So we have additional photos and we have better quality. I see as a problem here the source of these photographs. This is my concern. Secondly, the OTP already had these photograph, and I think they were shown to Witness Brakovic, I think. And I had the same objection to the authenticity of these photographs as to the time when they were made, who shot them, et cetera. And I believe that I still have the same problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That problem is overcome if the witness is able to say he can identify what is depicted in the photograph. I've known from a couple of times when you've made objections that there may be a different practice to which you are used in your jurisdiction. But here if a witness is shown a photograph, he looked at it, and he says, Goodness, yes, that's a photograph of Mr. Djurdjic. I know him well. We can receive that photograph here even if we don't know who took the photograph, where it was taken, and whether you were with somebody else or not on the day, to just illustrate the point. So if your only concern is that you've not been provided with those details, that may not be a complete objection to the receipt of them, especially in respect of those several photographs which have already been received into evidence but in a lesser-quality form.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I understand everything you say, but I don't know who's on the photograph so the witness can tell me, This is Tom, Dick, or Harry, and I don't know what to compare it to. I can't judge who that person is. I don't know who took the photograph and what is being recognised. That's a problem. And another problem is if the photograph is authentic. If it's just person A, B, or C and we know that they are A, B, or C, he can confirm what he knows, yes, this is A. Thank you for the explanation. However, it's up to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Gopalan, anything to add about the authenticity of the photograph?

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: The only thing I'd add, Your Honours, is in relation to the additional photographs, these were referred to -- the report itself was referred to by Mr. Abrahams during his testimony, both the report and the book were referred to by Mr. Abrahams during his testimony, and he provides an explanation there as to who took the photographs. So that information is already at hand. And in any event, as mentioned by Your Honours, the intention of showing the photographs to the witness is purely for the -- for identification provided by the witness in relation to what's depicted in those photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So the witnesses to whom they are to be shown are people are whom, in your expectation, will be able to identify the subject matter depicted in each photograph?

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours, because the report and the book relate to the incidents in the village of Cuska, and these two individuals are from that village, and therefore the experience, the contents of the report, and the book first-hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there something else, Mr. Djurdjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to respond to what my learned friend has said. The photographs have been in the possession of the Prosecution since 2001, and in the notification I received it says that it is not known from whom the photographs were received, even the Human Rights Watch cannot guarantee for their authenticity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you able to add anything to that, Ms. Gopalan?

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Firstly, Your Honours, I'm not entirely sure where the information about the photographs being in our possession since 2001 is from. And again in relation to the notification, I'm not able to comment on the authenticity and Human Rights Watch not being able to authenticate these photographs. Our position is simply that the report was admitted into evidence, there were no objections made to the source of that report at that point, and the photographs have now gone into evidence. We simply seek to add better photographs that will assist all parties. In relation to the additional photographs, as I mentioned, there is a reference in the transcript of Fredrick Abrahams as to who took those photographs. There's an explanation of the investigative process involved in relation to the taking of those photographs. And finally, the witnesses themselves were direct participants of the whole investigative process and therefore will be able to assist all parties as to what is depicted on the photographs, which is the intention I -- which is what we intend to use the photographs for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It is the Chamber's view that the photographs will be received. In respect of the three that are additional to the photographs we already have in evidence, the Chamber's view of the weight of them will, of course, be dependent upon what is said about them by the witnesses when they are viewed. We will now adjourn to continue on Monday, I believe, in the afternoon, and there is no other reason that I'm aware of that we shouldn't be able to proceed immediately to the evidence of that witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: We will be able to proceed immediately --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: -- based on the information I have at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. We hope to make faster progress next week. Could I mention that there will be delivered, I expect, on Monday the short written decision about the objections that were made to certain exhibits during the course of the evidence of an earlier witness. We adjourn now until Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 18th day of May, 2009, at 2.15 p.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
